body.text: UN climate conferences always come to an agreement in the end. They have to: with the fate of the Earth dependent on consensus among 196 nations, there is always some compromise everyone is prepared to accept to keep the show on the road.

Except this year. COP31 ended yesterday in Antalya, Turkey, with some minor issues decided but the main text lying in pieces on the conference floor. A full two days after the scheduled close — making it the longest-ever COP — it was apparent to everyone that no consensus could be reached and the joint presidencies, Turkey and Australia, had to concede an unprecedented failure.

The cause of the breakdown was at the same time largely symbolic and politically substantive. One hundred and thirty nations — the Europeans, most of the small islands and Latin Americans, and a number of the least-developed countries — insisted the final text had to include a global commitment to “transitioning away from fossil fuels.” This language was first agreed in a dramatic breakthrough at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 — the first time a COP had nailed fossil fuel use as the primary problem. But since then Saudi Arabia, Russia and other fossil fuel producers, along with some of their oil- and gas-importing allies, have been determined to ensure the phrase would never be used again — in a COP, in the G20, or in any other multilateral forum. They insisted it could not be repeated here.

This argument played out last year at COP30. The compromise eked out there was for the final text not to say “transitioning away from fossil fuels” but instead to refer to the COP28 decision in which it was embedded. In classic negotiating fashion, this allowed one side to say the language was absent and the other to say it was (implicitly) present.

But this year the countries committed to stronger climate action decided they were no longer prepared to put up with that. In a blistering press conference, Panama’s environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro complained that the world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia… but we have fallen in love with our kidnappers.” It was ludicrous that the COP, having agreed the world needed to transition away from fossil fuels — a statement of the scientifically obvious — should not be able to say it again. As a European delegate confessed: “The public already think these annual negotiations are a bit of a circus. Refusing to name fossil fuels as the problem just makes us look mad — or pathetic.”

In their newfound determination not to allow the fossil fuel producers to get their way, the countries of the so-called “High Ambition Coalition” were helped by the thinness of the rest of the COP agenda. It is easier to bring a conference down if there’s not much to lose in so doing. In this respect COP31 was the ideal meeting.

The brute fact is that there is not much for COPs to negotiate about these days. Over the last few years the technical rules of the 2015 Paris Agreement have all been agreed and the major legacy issues resolved. So the issues on the formal agenda this time looked thin. Some were irresolvable — the developed countries have no budgetary authority to commit to the specific annual sums they will pay developing countries between now and 2035, however much they are implored to do so. Others were largely meaningless, such as further non-binding words on the principles of a “just transition,” which every country will in reality do in its own way or not at all.

For this reason, Turkey and Australia decided early on that they would focus the COP31 negotiations on the overarching “cover decision” rather than the formal agenda. The introductory cover text is normally what diplomats call a “chapeau” to the main negotiated decisions: a combination of legal context and rhetorical flourish to give the whole thing a sense of coherence and overall purpose, but without any substantive content. But this year the cover decision became the main site of political argument.

This placed Australian climate and energy minister Chris Bowen centre stage. As chair of the negotiations he put himself in charge of both generating the cover text and then rewriting it to reflect countries’ different views. He and his co-president, Turkish environment minister Murat Kurum, issued three drafts of the cover decision during the second week; but instead of allowing countries to negotiate face to face over them, as would once have happened, they adopted the more recent practice of receiving individual country and group ministers in a time-consuming process of bilateral shuttle diplomacy. It left ministers and officials spending long hours simply waiting for the next draft to appear. Few of them appreciated this, and frustrations bubbled over.

Making the cover decision the centrepiece of COP had one advantage. As Bowen and Kurum intended, countries inserted into it issues that were not otherwise on the negotiating agenda. Three of these became the main bones of contention.

First, Australia and Turkey themselves insisted on the inclusion of a new energy target: that by 2035, 35 per cent of the world’s energy demand should be met by electricity. This “35 by 35” ambition was agreed earlier in the fortnight by a number of countries as part of the “Action Agenda” program taking place alongside the formal negotiations. But that didn’t mean all countries would be expected to agree to it in the cover text. The co-presidencies forced it through, however, noting that it added to the two existing energy commitments — to treble the world’s supply of renewables and double energy efficiency — agreed at previous COPs. Together these would demonstrate, Bowen said, not just that the world would now be shifting away from fossil fuels, but the means by which it would do so.

While supportive of the electricity target, the small island states wanted to go further. Electrification was not enough to cut emissions, they said; it must be electrification powered by renewables. This was not at all to the liking of the Arab Group and Russia, whose support for electrification is conditional on its continued powering by fossil fuels. So the final compromise text noted that the target should sit “alongside efforts to… increase clean energy.” And the fossil fuel producers ensured a strong commitment to carbon capture, use and storage as well.

A similar division between the small islands and Europeans on the one side, and the Arab Group and Russia on the other, characterised a second critical decision: the timing of the next report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC. The IPCC, which collates the work of the world’s climate scientists, is not governed by the COP, and the latter has never previously seen fit to criticise its work program. But this year the IPCC is under serious threat. Saudi Arabia, Russia and India are trying to delay publication of the report of the IPCC’s critical working group on climate policy to try to ensure that it does not come out before the next “global stocktake,” in 2028.

The global stocktake is the five-yearly moment when the COP reviews the evidence of climate science and decides how the world should respond. (It was at the last stocktake that the goal of “transitioning away from fossil fuels” was agreed.) A vital resource for this process is the most recent assessment of the IPCC, in which it considers the latest scientific papers and offers governments an impartial analysis of their findings. The IPCC has three working groups: on the state of the climate itself; on the impacts of climate change; and on the policy measures which can most effectively respond to them. The first two are expected to report before the 2028 stocktake, but the third is being held up by countries which don’t wish to be pressured into acting by its conclusions.

This has deeply angered those committed to further climate action. Without the report of working group 3, the recalcitrant countries will claim that the 2028 global stocktake lacks sufficient information to make recommendations on global action. So the High Ambition Coalition inserted into the COP31 cover text an unprecedented call for the IPCC to ensure the policy report would be ready in time. But a rearguard action was fought by the Saudis, Russians and Indians and after five days of wrangling they succeeded in keeping specific mention of working group 3 out of the final text. It was another reason for its rejection.

The third issue was perhaps the most significant of all. In previous COPs, delegates regularly made impassioned pleas for deeper emissions cuts in order to “keep 1.5 alive,” referring to the Paris Agreement goal of holding global warming to no more than 1.5C above pre-industrial times. But 1.5 is on its deathbed. The global temperature rise has already reached 1.4C and will surpass 1.5 as a ten-year average some time before 2030.

We are therefore now in a world of “overshoot” — the official name for an emissions and temperature trajectory that takes the world past 1.5C, but could still return to it later in the century. Acknowledgement of this was not on the formal COP agenda; but most countries recognised that it had to be done. And not just by referencing overshoot: the COP, they said, had to state for the first time that emissions reduction is no longer enough. When emissions reach net zero, the world cannot stop. To cool the planet back to 1.5C we will have to start on the path of “negative emissions,” that is, taking carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere.

No COP has ever said this before. And it takes the UN into uncharted territory. What technologies for carbon dioxide removal, or CDR, will be allowed? Who will be allowed to do it, under what regulatory regime? Who will pay for it?

Few countries have even begun contemplating the answers to these questions: but many insisted here that they must be asked. So the cover text included the first ever recognition by a COP of the necessity of CDR and of managing its development and implementation. With next year’s COP presidency Ethiopia having joined a new (small) club of countries committed to “net negative emissions,” we can expect much further discussion about this at COP32 in Addis Ababa.

In theory, rejection of the cover text means that none of these three issues have been decided upon. But in a strange way this hardly matters. They have been put on the agenda, and they are not going to go away.
And this raises an interesting question. Can a COP be more successful when it fails than when it succeeds?

Climate action is a battle on two fronts. On the one hand it’s a painstaking process in which governments make complex public policy, businesses and financiers invest in solutions, and economic behaviours and emissions outcomes gradually change. On the other it’s a visceral political struggle in which advocates of climate action are in a constant argument with its opponents. On a daily basis the advocates try to persuade the public that any short-term pain will be more than compensated by the long-term gain, while the opponents big up the costs and insist that, since no other country is doing anything, it’s all a waste of money and effort anyway.

In the first battle, formal COP decisions are important. They provide guidance to policymakers and market signals to business investors. But COPs are also a vital weapon in the second battle. Once a year leaders are forced to go and make a speech in favour of more ambitious climate action. The media report on the argument between the fossil fuel industry and an otherwise incomprehensible coalition of Pacific islanders, green business leaders and young campaigners. Tens of thousands of such people gain inspiration and energy from networking and exchanging ideas in a global climate festival and trade fair.

And now we have the negotiation on the cover decision to bring the political battle into sharp relief. It would have been better if the COP31 cover decision had been agreed. But the disagreement itself is a political signal. In the full glare of global media publicity it makes clear the faultline of climate politics. On the one side, two-thirds of the world’s countries are now committed to transitioning away from fossil fuels. On the other, one-third are desperate to hang on to the export revenues and geopolitical relationships that come with deep oil and gas reserves and the need to consume them.

This faultline has long been there, but previous COPs have managed to paper over it with ambiguous language and uneasy compromise. In Antalya that process seems to have come to the end of its road. Paradoxically, this COP’s failure might have been what the world needed. •
